title: Study 2's three sentences contradict each other, and Figure 1(b) sides with the third
location: published p. 2, Figure 1(b); p. 3, the paragraph on Study 2
published: When their party controls 60 percent of seats (compared with 40 percent), Republicans prefer a candidate who is more conservative. When their party controls 60 percent of seats (compared with 40 percent), Democrats prefer a candidate who is less liberal. Surprisingly (to me at least), subjects of both parties want more moderate candidates when the Republicans are in the majority and more extreme candidates when the Democrats are in the majority.
note: The first two sentences put both parties' subjects further from the center when Republicans hold the majority: Republicans turn more conservative and Democrats more liberal. The third says the reverse. Figure 1(b) agrees with the third. Its scale runs from 1 = Extreme Republican to 5 = Extreme Democrat, and it plots Republican at 0.212 and Democrat at -0.121. The 2018 survey agrees with the first two. Democrats (1 to 3 on the seven-point scale) come to 0.212 weighted and 0.067 unweighted, Republicans (5 to 7) to -0.049 and -0.045, and all four intervals cover zero. Swapped labels in Figure 1(b) would explain part of this, since the weighted Democratic estimate lies within 0.001 of the mark labeled Republican. The mark labeled Democrat is unexplained: none of the specifications we tried gives it credibly. We therefore cannot say which sentence is wrong or why, and this item corrects nothing.
